title: How a barometer reads the weather in the weight of air
description: Air has weight, and its mood swings move a needle. How a barometer turns invisible pressure into a forecast you can read on the wall.

body.heading: The ocean of air above us
paragraphs: We live at the bottom of an ocean of air. It presses on everything — on your shoulders right now sits a column of air reaching to the top of the atmosphere — and that pressure changes as weather systems pass overhead.

A barometer measures that pressure. In the earliest designs, from the 1640s, air pressure pushed on a pool of mercury and forced it up a glass tube; the height of the mercury column was the reading. Later aneroid barometers replaced the liquid with a small sealed metal box that flexes as pressure changes and moves a needle.

body.heading: Rising fair, falling rain
paragraphs: High pressure usually means sinking, settling air — the recipe for calm, clear weather. Low pressure means rising air, which cools, forms clouds and often brings rain and wind. So a barometer's needle drifting up is a hopeful sign, and a needle falling fast is the sky clearing its throat.

The instrument does not see the future; it reads the present so well that the future gives itself away. Sailors watched barometers obsessively, because a sudden fall at sea was an early warning no lookout could match.

body.heading: Read one like a sailor
paragraphs: Tap the glass gently and note not just where the needle sits, but where it has been: barometers carry a marker hand you set each morning so the day's drift is visible at a glance. Change over hours matters more than the number itself.
Pair the reading with a look out of the window for a week, and you will start forecasting like a local — because that, in the end, is all a forecast is: pressure, pattern and practice.

takeaway: A barometer weighs the air: rising pressure usually brings settled weather, a fast fall warns of wind and rain.
